source.title: Fast and Multiphase Rates for Nearest Neighbor Classifiers

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies nearest-neighbor classification error as a function of dataset size. It does not test language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling, prediction of larger language-model runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses scaling laws and cites prior language- and vision-model work, but those cited results are not its own. Its own results concern classification error for k-NN classifiers, not the language-model losses or allocations named in the claim. The k-NN findings are recorded under fits_no_version; no claim version is tested.
record.test_reason: The study analyses k-NN classification excess risk as training-set size grows, using theorems plus MNIST/F-MNIST and synthetic logistic plots. It trains no language or other neural models and measures no pretraining loss, compute allocation, architecture shape or downstream task scaling. It cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. Its multiphase-rate finding concerns a different kind of system, a nonparametric classifier, so it bears on no claim version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that k-NN test error rates are not uniform across sample-size ranges. On benign problems (standard logistic, Gaussian design) k-NN reaches the minimax-optimal parametric O(d/n) rate. A slightly modified problem yields a fast-then-slow two-phase rate, with the slow phase provably unavoidable. They propose extending such analyses to neural networks as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes k-NN classification error as training dataset size varies; it does not reproduce the language-model loss-scaling or compute-allocation methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported rate depends on the data distribution: the standard Gaussian-design logistic problem has a parametric excess-risk bound, while the modified logistic problem has a two-phase bound. The modified-model analysis uses k = n3/4, and the authors state the choice can be generalized to nγ for γ ∈ (1/2, 1).

fits_no_version.finding: For k-NN on Gaussian-design logistic regression, expected excess risk is at most cd/n when k=⌊c0 n⌋ and d ≥ C log n. This matches the minimax lower bound order (Theorem 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonparametric k-NN classifiers can attain parametric, dimension-polynomial error rates on benign distributions.

fits_no_version.finding: For a modified logistic model, k-NN excess risk decays fast down to about 0.45, then slowly as n^{-1/(4d)} (Theorem 4). A constant lower bound holds for n ≤ exp(c1 d/log d) (Theorem 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dataset-size scaling of classification error can be multiphase, with a fast early phase and a provably slow later phase depending on the data distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Nearest-neighbor test error on F-MNIST initially tracks MNIST, then slows at larger sample sizes (Figure 1, qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Similar datasets can show diverging error-scaling rates at larger sample sizes for the same learner.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted for presentation at the Conference on Learning Theory (COLT) 2025
record.problems: The image-dataset curves are described qualitatively, with no numerical values or uncertainty stated in the text. The paper's results concern k-NN classification rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-specific results were reported. Figure 2's synthetic logistic-regression experiments are discussed qualitatively and overlap with the theoretical results recorded in R1–R4; their plotted values were not extracted as additional rows.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small to large training runs.
All: no depth/width or architecture-shape comparison.
No neural image, video, repeated-data or fine-tuning scaling. The MNIST/F-MNIST results are for k-NN classifiers only.
All: no downstream task performance versus scale or loss.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits for language models. The multiphase (bending) curves are for k-NN classification error only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is right. The only link to the claim is the motivating citation of Kaplan et al. and ViT scaling. Several row values in R2–R4 were mangled in text extraction; corrected readings are given in row_fixes. Figure 2's synthetic curves are declared in rows_left_out and bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation for language models.
Effects of depth, width, or architecture details on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the specified language-model power-law form transfers to other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of language-model downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.
